title: VILA: Analytic Learning with Vision-Language Calibration
one_liner: Keep a frozen language model as an anchor while learning task-specific features analytically, and use language word-meanings to fix prediction errors.
lead: Class-incremental learning means teaching a model new tasks without forgetting old ones. When using a pre-trained model, the usual approach is to tweak its weights by running tiny adjustment steps (a method that computes which way to nudge each number, which way shrinks error the most), but this accumulates errors across tasks. VILA takes a different path: it keeps one branch frozen as a stable anchor and learns a second branch analytically (via closed-form math instead of slow iterative steps), while using language models as a safety net to catch and correct prediction mistakes.

problem.h2: Analytic learning breaks when features become rigid
paras: Analytic learning is fast: instead of running thousands of tiny nudges (gradient descent), you solve one equation to find the exact best weights. But it has a fatal weakness. When you train a model on a fixed pre-trained backbone, that backbone does not change, so the feature space stays locked. New tasks see the same frozen feature dimensions they saw before. If a new task needs to stretch or rotate the feature space to separate its classes, it cannot. The features become a cage.

A beginner might just add more layers to learn on top of the frozen features. That fails because the new task's classes do not map cleanly onto the frozen space, so the model guesses wrong. You are stuck between two choices: freeze the backbone and fail (rigidity), or unfreeze it and watch all your old knowledge disappear (catastrophic forgetting).

callout.html: Analytic learning trades speed for feature rigidity; the frozen backbone cannot adapt to new tasks, so predictions stay misaligned.

For uncertain cases, retrieve language word-lists of top-K predicted classes and use them to correct the model's guess.

paras: VILA modifies the feature representation by fusing two sources: the frozen pre-trained backbone and a learned task-specific adapter. Instead of relying on one rigid space, it geometrically merges both into a single combined list of numbers that grows richer with each new task.

hidden.name: alignment drift
paras: When a new task arrives, its class pattern does not align with the frozen feature space. VILA measures how misaligned the new task is by computing the distance between the new task's data spread and the main directions the old task learned. This distance captures rigidity: a large distance means the frozen space is too far from where the new task needs to be.

The paper estimates this distance by comparing where the new task's data points should project in the learned space versus where they actually land. Smaller distance means the frozen features work well; larger distance means the task needs adaptation. By fusing the learnable branch, VILA shrinks this distance, bringing the effective feature space closer to where new tasks need it.

heat.caption: Darker means more misalignment; marked cells show the new task before and after fusion.

reads.html: As new tasks arrive, their data spreads in different directions than old tasks did. The frozen backbone was trained on old data, so it has not learned to recognize new task's patterns. Fusion closes this gap by adding a plastic branch that learns the new direction.

The paper maximizes likelihood over the learned subspace during task 1 training, aligning features S1 with task 1's main directions. For task t, leftover errors capture how far the new task drifts from this learned foundation. Geometric calibration projects this error into the hybrid space, reducing accumulated misalignment.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: closed-form math meets language anchors
paras: The core trick is asymmetry. One branch stays frozen (the language model, a universal visual anchor). The other branch is free to learn. When you have both, you can write a single equation that solves for the new task's class weights without any gradient loops. The frozen branch keeps old knowledge safe; the learned branch adapts to the new class patterns.

At the feature level, geometric calibration merges them by treating the frozen features and learned features as two subspaces and finding the best linear blend that minimizes error on new examples. This is a one-step solve, not a loop. At the decision level, the language model acts as a referee: when the combined model is uncertain about which class it is (top predictions are close), the text encoder votes on the class names themselves, anchored in language understanding. Words carry built-in knowledge (learned during training on billions of sentences) that the raw features might miss.

stages.s: New task data and class labels
Geometric calibration fuses both via one equation
Analytic solver finds class weights (no iterations)

math.words: merged_vector = alpha * frozen_features + (1 - alpha) * learned_features. Then solve for class_weight = inverse_of_covariance * correlation_with_labels (standard closed-form solution).
math.equation: F_t = alpha * F_frozen + (1 - alpha) * F_learned; W_new = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose frozen features are [0.8, 0.6] for an image, learned features are [0.2, 0.4] (different direction).
Calibration finds alpha = 0.7 (favor the frozen branch more).
Now train on 10 examples of the new class with this merged space: the pseudo-inverse (X^T X)^-1 X^T solves in one step for the weight that best separates the class.
No loops, no gradient noise. Done.

math.note: The first term is the frozen anchor (stability); the second is the plastic learner (adaptation). The balance alpha is set during calibration on the first task and never changes, ensuring slow forgetting of old knowledge.

items.b: The learned adapter becomes a crutch.
items.html: If you train the adapter on too many tasks, it starts to overfit and no longer truly learns task-specific features. The fusion becomes unstable. Solution: freeze the adapter after task 1, do not update it.

If the text encoder was trained on different class names or domains than your data (e.g., a bird classifier using CLIP trained on generic English text), the language vote is weak. For domain-specific tasks, the word-meanings learned by the encoder are less reliable.

If the frozen features and learned features have very different scales (one much larger than the other), the calibration blend becomes sensitive to small alpha changes. Solution: normalize both branches to the same scale before fusion.

Train the adapter only on task 1, keep it frozen after. Fuse geometrically with careful calibration. Cache language word-lists offline. Use language voting only for top-K uncertain cases, not for every prediction.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulator that takes a simple dataset (e.g., CIFAR10 split into 5 tasks: two classes per task, arriving one task at a time). Implement VILA: (1) train a small adapter on task 1 and freeze it; (2) for each new task, compute the geometric blend and solve analytically; (3) use a CLIP text encoder to refine predictions. Compare against a gradient-based fine-tuning baseline. Measure both old-task accuracy (how much did you forget?) and new-task accuracy (how well did you learn?).
demo.metric_eq: forgetting = (old_task_accuracy_at_task_1) - (old_task_accuracy_at_task_5); vila_forgetting should be much smaller than baseline_forgetting.
demo.closing: The demo must show that VILA remembers old tasks far better than gradient-based methods (because the frozen branch never moves), while still learning new tasks nearly as well (the learned branch adapts), all without iterative training loops.
